The Montana constitution reserves to the people the powers of initiative and referendum. CI-133
amends the constitution to secure this fundamental right from interference by the government.
Speciﬁcally, CI-133 requires impartial, predictable, open, and timely processes for ballot issues.
Petitions and ballot statements must be approved within 90 days of the initial submission, and legal
challenges to ballot qualiﬁcation must be resolved before the deadline for ﬁnalizing ballots. CI-133
requires the state to allow ample time for signature gathering, prohibits disqualiﬁcation of petitions
because of minor or technical issues, allows voters to withdraw their signatures if they so choose,
and prohibits the use of government resources to support or oppose a ballot measure.

I-194, if passed, limits the powers of artificial persons to those powers necessary or convenient as
provided by law. These powers must exclude contributing anything of value to candidate elections,
supporting or opposing political parties, or supporting or opposing state or local ballot issues.
Artificial persons include non-profits, trusts, partnerships, corporations, trade associations, or
unincorporated associations and includes all such entities doing business in Montana. Any
violation of I-194 is punished by forfeiting all privileges to do business in Montana. Those
privileges may be, but are not automatically, restored upon disgorgement and certification of
compliance with I-194. I-194 does not apply to the distribution of news, commentary, or editorial
content. I-194 also does not apply to the state of Montana, political subdivisions, individuals,
political committees, or public corporations.

measures.questionText:
CI-132 amends the Montana Constitution to require that judicial elections remain nonpartisan.

[] YES on Constitutional Amendment CI-132

[] NO on Constitutional Amendment CI-132

provenance.quote:
CI-132 amends the Montana Constitution to require that judicial elections remain nonpartisan.

[] YES on Constitutional Amendment CI-132

[] NO on Constitutional Amendment CI-132

argumentsFor:
Judges should be elected based on their record and qualifications, not politics.
Constitutional Initiative 132 protects the high value we as Montanans place on impartial
judges free from political influence. CI-132 is a one-sentence initiative that simply
ensures that judicial elections in Montana remain nonpartisan.
CI-132 helps everyday Montanans.
Most Montanans interact with judges in family, traffic, civil, and criminal courts, which
decide everything from child custody to employment and property disputes. There is no
Republican or Democratic way to handle these cases – there’s only the law. Mixing politics
with these everyday cases will hurt Montanans who just want an unbiased, fair hearing
without worrying about politics influencing the judge’s decision.
CI-132 protects the impartiality of our judges and our courts.
Politicians in Helena recently passed House Bill 39, a law allowing political parties to
contribute up to nearly $90,000 to Montana judicial candidates. That’s a dangerous step
toward making judges cater to political parties. Politics today runs on money, and we need
to protect our courtrooms. We need independent courts with judges who remain
impartial and accountable to the constitution, not politics.
CI-132 has broad support.
Nine retired members of the Montana Supreme Court are backing this proposal alongside
Montana legal experts, retired sheriffs, and criminal prosecutors. More than 100,000
Montanans from every county signed the petition to get this issue on the ballot. Montanans
know that we must keep the power over our courts in the hands of Montana citizens and
ensure our judges are fair, unbiased, and accountable to us.
CI-132 keeps judges accountable to Montanans.
Montanans began electing judges in nonpartisan elections in 1935 in response to the
powerful Copper Kings who were buying judges to rule in their favor. This simple measure
protects that longstanding tradition so we can keep judges accountable to the people’s
interests, not deep-pocketed political interests.
Vote YES on CI-132 to ensure our judicial elections remain nonpartisan, keep our
judges impartial, and make sure politics stays out of our courts.

Approval Committee: Jeffrey Sherlock, Craig J. Anderson, Katherine “Kitty” Curtis

Montanans have selected fair and impartial judges in nonpartisan elections for over 90
years. That’s because we believe that judges should be elected based on their record
and qualifications, not politics.
Voting “yes” on CI-132 means Montana citizens can hold judges accountable to “we the
people” instead of politics. Our country's founders knew that an independent judiciary was
essential for a free republic. CI-132 helps keep our courts independent of the politics that
dominate the other branches of government.
Courts should be fair to everyone who stands before them, no matter what they're worth or
who they know. But politics today runs on money, and we can't let that into our
courtrooms. Justice shouldn't be for sale, and CI-132 helps keep money-driven politics out
of our courts.
As two retired District Court judges and a retired Dawson County Sheriff, we know Montana
voters aren’t fools. There is no Republican or Democratic way to handle cases like child
custody, employment, or property disputes - there’s only the law and the Constitution.
Montana provides voters with an independent judicial performance report about every
judicial candidate’s experience, courtroom conduct, and decisions. For generations,
Montanans have cast their vote based on a judge's record and qualifications – why do
opponents want to bring politics into our courts?
Vote YES on CI-132 to:
• Ensure judges are elected based on their record and qualifications.
• Keep money-driven politics out of our courts.
• Ensure Montanans can get a fair and impartial trial without worrying about
politics.

Approval Committee: Jeffrey Sherlock, Craig J. Anderson, Katherine “Kitty” Curtis
argumentsAgainst:
CI-132 is not what it seems. It has nothing to do with keeping courts impartial. Actually, it is
an anti-transparency measure.
Have you ever been frustrated by the lack of information about the candidates for judge?
That’s because the current system—which CI-132 would make permanent—isn’t
transparent. It forces Montanans to vote with a blindfold on. It prevents us from learning
crucial facts about the candidates.
Why would anyone want to do this? According to the authoritative website Ballotpedia, CI132 is largely funded from out-of-state special interests based in places like New York City
and Washington, D.C. They’ve already spent over $2 million to sell us this bill of goods,
and apparently plan to spend a lot more.
Don’t let them fool you.
We all want impartial courts, and most judges do try to be impartial. But let’s face it: Like
most other people, judicial candidates usually have political party preferences. So before
we vote, we are entitled to know what those preferences are.
But CI-132 would deny us that information—forever.
Thomas Jefferson said, “Whenever the people are well-informed, they can be trusted with
their own government.” By contrast, CI-132 enshrines ignorance in the Montana
constitution. That's bad for Montana, bad for the justice system, and bad for democracy.
The proponents of CI-132 don’t trust you with your own government.
Tell the rich out-of-state special interests to pick up their cash and go home. Montanans
decide what happens in Montana!
Vote “NO” on CI-132 and let the sun shine in!

Rejection Committee: Robert “Rob” Natelson, David Knobel, Derek Oestreicher,
Representative Greg Overstreet, Duncan Scott

If you are reading this rebuttal, you are precisely the type of voter that CI-132 seeks to
blindfold—an informed voter. The out-of-state special interests pushing CI-132 have spent
over $2 million to lock you into a broken system. What are they trying to hide?
They want to hide how these same special interest groups pour money into judicial
campaigns.The false “non partisan” label hides this dark money from voters.
The truth is that judges have political leanings. They are human after all. Judges don’t
transcend ordinary existence and become blind to politics once they put on a black robe. If
the out-of-state special interests truly want judges elected based on their record,
they would want voters informed about a candidate’s entire record—which necessarily
includes political leanings. Why do these out-of-state special interests want you to have
less information?
The “non partisan” label has not made our state supreme court more impartial. On the
contrary, the Montana Supreme Court, among other defects, has been repeatedly
identified as biased. Nor is it surprising that former judges and certain attorneys—who
have perhaps benefitted from this broken system—would prefer that voters remain
uninformed.
Voters like you—who take the time to read about the candidates and issues—should think
twice about supporting CI-132. Would you vote while wearing a blindfold? Or, would you
prefer to make informed choices about judicial candidates?
Vote “no” on CI-132 and let the sun shine in!

Rejection Committee: Robert “Rob” Natelson, David Knobel, Derek Oestreicher,
Representative Greg Overstreet, Duncan Scott

measures.questionText:
The Montana constitution reserves to the people the powers of initiative and referendum. CI-133
amends the constitution to secure this fundamental right from interference by the government.
Speciﬁcally, CI-133 requires impartial, predictable, open, and timely processes for ballot issues.
Petitions and ballot statements must be approved within 90 days of the initial submission, and legal
challenges to ballot qualiﬁcation must be resolved before the deadline for ﬁnalizing ballots. CI-133
requires the state to allow ample time for signature gathering, prohibits disqualiﬁcation of petitions
because of minor or technical issues, allows voters to withdraw their signatures if they so choose,
and prohibits the use of government resources to support or oppose a ballot measure.

representative government and invites abuse of the ballot process. CI-133 is a trojan horse

good evidence that Montana has a healthy initiative process. Why would we “fix” a system

initiative passes, it becomes binding law for a minimum of two years before it can be
changed or undone.

constitutional, transparent, and won’t bankrupt the state. CI-133 scraps these
commonsense protections, making it easier for well-funded special interests and paid
signature gatherers to place poorly-drafted measures on the ballot.

directly vote on popular ideas when elected officials aren’t responsive to voters’
desires. Today, though, special interests have discovered the process also allows them to

gatherers, most of whom are working for companies that collect north of $1 million

days,” reports the Helena IR.

personally vouch that the process was not overly difficult. As a rancher, I fix broken

works. CI-133 is unnecessary.

process. That’s a winning proposal for groups with $1 million or more to spend buying the

Overstreet, Charles Robison

democratic, but organized and wealthy interests—sometimes from out of state—
often drive them. Collecting signatures is expensive and usually needs paid workers.

initiatives have passed popular ideas, but CI-133 would make it harder for elected
lawmakers (who answer to voters) to ﬁx problems or update laws.

signatures, review legality, stop fraud, and run elections smoothly. Strict new rules
could cause rushed reviews, endless lawsuits over vague phrases like “minor
mistakes” or “ample time,” and confusion for election workers.

balances. Initiatives are a helpful backup tool, not the main way to govern.

would make future improvements to the initiative process much harder.

voterGuide.summary:
The Montana constitution reserves to the people the powers of initiative and referendum.
CI-133 amends the constitution to secure this fundamental right from interference by the
government. Speciﬁcally, CI-133 requires impartial, predictable, open, and timely
processes for ballot issues. Petitions and ballot statements must be approved within 90
days of the initial submission, and legal challenges to ballot qualiﬁcation must be resolved
before the deadline for ﬁnalizing ballots. CI-133 requires the state to allow ample time for
signature gathering, prohibits disqualiﬁcation of petitions because of minor or technical
issues, allows voters to withdraw their signatures if they so choose, and prohibits the use of
government resources to support or oppose a ballot measure.

argumentsFor:
The Montana Plan, I-194, will end the ability of artificial persons (such as corporations,
associations, unions) to spend to support or oppose candidates and ballot issues in
Montana.
The 2024 presidential election year saw a total of $14.8 billion spent on federal campaigns:
$9.5 billion on congressional races and $5.3 billion on the presidential race. In contrast,
the entire general fund budget for the state of Montana in 2026 was $3.5 billion, less than a
quarter of the amount of money spent on federal campaigns.
That amount of money alone makes it critically important to understand where that money
is coming from and who is bankrolling campaigns.
Money spent to influence the decision of a voter without being required to disclose the
original donor is referred to as “dark money.” The source is often concealed from the
public - but not the politicians.
Anonymous “dark money” is typically used to pay for incessant digital ads, mailers and
television that are intended, on the one hand, to negatively attack and “carpet bomb” an
opposing candidate with grainy photographs and insinuations of corruption or
incompetence; or, on the other hand, to elevate the opposing candidate whose alleged
attributes and competencies are inflated but alleged to be indispensable to the existence
of the country. Neither representation is completely accurate nor helpful for voters trying in
good faith to determine the best candidate to serve the public good.
In the 2024 Montana Senate race, outside groups, including super PACs, spent $162.7
million on independent expenditures, including mailers, TV ads, and digital and socialmedia advertising. Just one “dark money” group alone, The Last Best Place PAC,
sponsored approximately 39,000 ad airings in Montana, and neither Montana voters or
candidates had any idea where its money came from. It had been intentionally shrouded in
a tangled web to generate confusion and disarray among Montana voters.
Business corporations can transfer money directly to super PACs and other outside
groups. In 2024, Koch Industries, for example, spent $49 million, $40 million of which went
to Americans for Prosperity Action, which, in turn, spent money on Montana elections.
Artificial persons (such as business corporations, nonprofits, and unions) are neither
constitutional nor human creatures. They are pure creations of state law. Montana grants
them every power they have. And Montana has reserved the authority to modify those
powers at any time, for any reason.

If I-194 is passed by the people, Montana will no longer grant artificial persons the power to
spend in Montana's politics. It's that simple. No longer would anonymous "dark money" be
allowed in Montana campaigns - every dollar would be from a human person, would be
disclosed, and would be voluntary. If corporate officers and the great titans of business
and industry decide to spend money to support a candidate or an issue, they’ll have to do it
the same way the rest of us do. They’ll have to use their own money, observe contribution
limits, comply with reporting requirements, and disclose their name.
Approval Committee: Gary Buchanan, Marc Racicot, Raymond Jon Tester

Read the opposition statement and notice what it leaves out: Montana’s experience with
elections ﬂooded and distorted by outside secret money with no regard for the truth nor
issues Montanans face every day: healthcare, housing, taxes, schools, utility bills, and
public lands. Instead, they resort to scare tactics in a twisted attempt to portray the
defenders of unlimited “dark” money political spending as the underdogs and Montanans
reclaiming their elections as the threat. It’s the same old bait and switch Montanans have
seen before.
Elections should be decided by the votes of Montanans, not the dark money spent by
anonymous donors and corporations.
The opposition falsely claims that dark-money groups could continue spending as they do
now. Another bait and switch. I-194 eliminates the power of all artiﬁcial persons—including
501(c)(4) dark-money groups—to spend money supporting or opposing candidates and
ballot issues.
They also falsely suggest businesses and community groups could not even publish a
website. That is absurd. They may speak, organize, publish, and advocate on any issue they
choose. But, when they spend to support or oppose a candidate or ballot issue, they must
do so through a transparent political committee so voters can see who funds the message.
Small-business owners, church members, union members, employees, and nonproﬁt
supporters keep their individual voices.
Ruggedly independent Montanans once stood up to the Copper Kings . . . and we can do so
again by ending anonymous and corporate money in our elections.
I-194 serves the people of Montana.

Approval Committee: Gary Buchanan, Marc Racicot, Raymond Jon Tester
argumentsAgainst:
I-194 has nothing to do with protecting elections, removing money from politics, getting rid
of the inﬂuence of money in politics, or addressing undisclosed dark money spending.
Instead, it’s a misguided, poorly drafted, authoritarian attempt to unconstitutionally restrict
Montanans’ free speech rights under the guise of targeting spending in elections—even
though there isn’t a single example provided of corporate election spending but examples
abound of PAC and dark money spending that would continue to be allowed under I-194.
I-194 allows individuals to continue to spend unlimited amounts on elections and PAC and
many dark money groups to operate just as they do now. But it would target small Montana
businesses, churches, and community groups, and similar groups—referred to as “artiﬁcial
persons” in the measure—even though these entities are just groups of individual
Montanans. If such a group voices an opinion—whether by printing a pamphlet, running an
advertisement, creating a ﬁlm, or even maintaining a website—I-194 threatens extreme
penalties, including the loss of legal protections that could expose Montanans to personal
liability and put their personal assets at risk
Federal courts have already struck down twice similar laws as unconstitutional restrictions
on free speech, and the result would be the same here. If I-194 passes, it will accomplish
little beyond wasting Montana taxpayer dollars while it is tied up in court and ultimately
struck down.
The United States Supreme Court has already decided that the government cannot directly
ban a group of Montanans from engaging in political speech. In a famous case, a group of
individuals wanted to show a documentary about a presidential candidate during a
campaign, but federal law barred them because they acted through an organization rather
than as a single individual. The group sued under the First Amendment. The Supreme Court
decided that political speech during a campaign for public office is the core type of speech
protected by the First Amendment and determined that the government banning a
documentary about a candidate was a violation of free speech whether the documentary
was made by an individual or a group of individuals. I-194 seeks to accomplish the same
result of banning political speech during elections, not by directly banning it, but instead by
imposing extreme penalties on any group of Montanans who choose to engage in free
speech. The government cannot, and should not, be allowed to impose bans on free
speech during elections, directly or indirectly, and for that reason Montanans should reject
I-194 and vote no.

Rejection Committee: David Knobel, Matthew Dolphay, Todd O’Hair, Representative Greg
Overstreet, Dale Schowengerdt

“The Montana Plan” claims to end dark money and corporate inﬂuence in Montana
elections. It does neither. It imposes sweeping, unconstitutional restrictions on the freespeech rights of Montana small businesses, churches, and community groups, while
leaving untouched the out-of-state PACs and dark money that dominate Montana
campaigns. I-194 is a sham.
Proponents have not identiﬁed a single Montana corporation that has spent money to
inﬂuence a Montana election. Instead they point to Koch Industries and national super
PACs — entities Montana has no power to regulate. Their "creature of state law" theory only
works, by their own logic, for corporations Montana itself charters. The only entities I194 actually restricts are Montana’s own small businesses, ranches, churches, and
community groups, exposed to steep penalties for speaking up.
Courts, including the U.S. Supreme Court, have already rejected this theory. In First
National Bank of Boston v. Bellotti, the Court struck down a nearly identical Massachusetts
law, holding the First Amendment protects political speech regardless of corporate
source; Citizens United v. FEC reaffirmed it. I-194 asks voters to relitigate a settled question
— and pay the legal bills when it loses again.
The irony: I-194’s own campaign is bankrolled by dark money, much of it from out of state,
funneled through the Transparent Election Initiative, a nonproﬁt that need not disclose its
donors, with help from a Washington, D.C. advocacy group.
Montanans deserve real transparency, not a doomed measure that punishes local
businesses while true outside spending goes untouched. Vote no on I-194.

Overstreet, Dale Schowengerdt
